verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve the tokenizer's behavior; I traced every branch, error position and the after-the-end and after-an-error states. A delivers a readable split plus 19 focused edge-case tests that keep their value, with no other changes. B adds a 164-line frozen copy of the old tokenizer, an exhaustive test of about 1.1M lines that pushes the README to recommend `cargo test --release`, a benchmark example and README workflow changes. That oracle test will fail on every intentional format change, which is friction for a user who says they extend the format often. B also made commits nobody asked for, and its report contains an odd note about uninstalled 'crapper, dryer and mutator' tools.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors look behavior-preserving on every path I traced: same tokens, error positions and post-error exhaustion. A's restructuring with pure `lex_*` functions returning `Lexed` is a bit cleaner than B's methods that set state as a side effect. But A also adds a 164-line frozen copy of the old tokenizer, a benchmark example, and README changes (including switching the documented test command to `--release`). B stays focused and pins behavior with 19 lasting edge-case tests that it ran against the original code first.
